344.title: The price of calm
344.hook: spilled oil, stolen wine: say, this is what peace of mind costs (Enchiridion 12)
344.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism treat small losses and annoyances as the price of tranquility, naming the cost and letting it go rather than stewing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: I gave it back. That was your line, too. Did you try the other verb when you were about to say I lost it? Day three hundred forty-four.

Somebody at work ate your yogurt from the office fridge. Your name was on it. In marker. You could spend the afternoon on this. Draft the passive-aggressive note. Investigate. Tell three people. Or you could do some quick math. The yogurt cost about a dollar. The afternoon of stewing costs a lot more. Epictetus did this math with olive oil and wine. Section twelve of the handbook puts a price tag on peace of mind, and the surprise is how cheap it is. Today: the price of calm.
screen: `THE STOLEN YOGURT.` → `THE AFTERNOON OF STEWING.` → `A PRICE TAG ON PEACE.`

segments.voice: First, the bargain. If you want to make progress, Epictetus says, drop thoughts like: if I don't watch my affairs, I'll have nothing to live on. Better, he says bluntly, to die of hunger free of grief and fear than to live in plenty and be troubled. That's strong, and he means it as a direction, not a test. Second, the kitchen. Begin with small things, he says. A little oil spilled. A little wine stolen. Say to yourself: this is the price of tranquility, the price of being undisturbed. Nothing is had for nothing. Third, the word. Tranquility here translates ataraxia: a, not, and a root meaning stirred up. Unstirred, like a pond on a still morning. Fourth, the servant, and an honest note. Epictetus finishes with a household scene: you call your servant and he may not come, or may come and do the wrong thing. He isn't so important, Epictetus says, that it's in his power to disturb you. Epictetus' examples come from a world where owning people was ordinary, and he had been enslaved himself. We can notice that plainly and still take the point that travels: other people's choices aren't a lever on your calm unless you hand it to them. So the yogurt. A dollar. That's the price. Paid gladly, it buys an afternoon back. Small days, small prices: a spilled cup here, a small unfairness there. The expensive part is refusing to pay.
screen: `BETTER HUNGRY THAN TROUBLED.` · `SPILLED OIL, STOLEN WINE.` · `ATARAXIA: UNSTIRRED.` · `NOBODY ELSE HOLDS THE LEVER.` · then, large: `THE PRICE OF CALM.`

segments.voice: Pick up something small within reach: a coin, a pen, a paper clip. Let it stand for one annoyance from today or yesterday. A spill, a late delivery, a parking ticket, the yogurt. Hold it in your palm and name its price, out loud or inside: this is what calm costs. A dollar, five minutes, a little pride. Then set the object down, the way you'd put coins on a counter. Paid. Sit with what you bought. The bell holds the time.
The price of calm. Epictetus' kitchen math: a little spilled oil, a little stolen wine, the small cost of staying undisturbed. Nothing is had for nothing. Today's word.
Your line: the price of calm. When a small loss comes today, let it go cheaply. Say the line, pay the price, and move on. Day three hundred forty-four.

345.title: Content to seem foolish
345.hook: if you want to improve, be willing to look foolish about outside things (Enchiridion 13)
345.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners deliberately accept looking uninformed or unfashionable about outside matters, as training in caring less about others' opinions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the price of calm. That was your line. When a small loss came, did you pay the price and move on? Day three hundred forty-five.

Athens. A merchant named Zeno, recently shipwrecked, has found a teacher: Crates the Cynic. The story comes from Diogenes Laertius. One day Crates hands him a pot of lentil soup and tells him to carry it through the busy potters' quarter. Zeno tries to hide the pot under his cloak, embarrassed. Crates cracks it with his staff, and soup runs down Zeno's legs. Zeno bolts. Crates calls after him, roughly: why run away, little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has happened to you. Zeno would go on to found the Stoic school. Today: content to seem foolish.
screen: `ZENO AND A POT OF SOUP.` → `CRATES CRACKS IT.` → `NOTHING TERRIBLE HAS HAPPENED.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. Section thirteen of the handbook says: if you want to make progress, be content to be thought foolish and simple about outside things. Not foolish about everything. About the outside things: the latest phone, the right restaurant, the gossip, who's up and who's down. Second, the harder half. Don't wish to be thought to know anything, Epictetus says. And if people start to think you're somebody, be suspicious of yourself. That's a striking line from a famous teacher. It sounds like Socrates in Plato's Apology, who says he is wiser only in not thinking he knows what he doesn't. Third, the reason. It isn't easy, he says, to keep your purpose in line with nature and also keep up with all the outside things. Care for one, and you're bound to neglect the other. Attention is limited. Spend it on looking clever and there's less left for being good. Fourth, why it's training. Looking foolish can feel like a small death. The red face, the wish to explain. That's exactly what Crates' soup pot was training. Each time you survive it, you learn the thing Crates shouted: nothing terrible has happened. You asked the obvious question in the meeting, and the meeting went on. You wore last year's coat, and the sun came up. You said I don't know, and someone finally explained it. People may think you're a little behind. Let them think it. Meanwhile, your attention is free for what's really yours.
screen: `FOOLISH ABOUT OUTSIDE THINGS.` · `DON'T WISH TO SEEM TO KNOW.` · `ATTENTION IS LIMITED.` · `NOTHING TERRIBLE HAS HAPPENED.` · then, large: `LET THEM THINK IT.`

segments.voice: Think of one place today where you usually perform knowing. A meeting, a class, a conversation about something you're supposed to understand. Picture yourself there, asking the simple question, or saying, I don't actually know what that means. Feel the flush of it. Let it rise and pass. Then hear Crates' line, gently this time: nothing terrible has happened. Decide where you'll try it for real. The bell holds the time.
Content to seem foolish. Epictetus' advice for anyone who wants to improve: let people think you simple about outside things, and keep your attention for what's yours. Today's word.
Your line: let them think it. Look foolish once today, on purpose and kindly: ask the obvious question, or admit you don't know. Day three hundred forty-five.

346.title: Who holds the leash
346.hook: whoever controls what you want is your master (Enchiridion 14)
346.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism notice which wants make them dependent on others, such as approval or replies, and practice wanting them less urgently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: content to seem foolish. Your line was let them think it. Did you ask the obvious question, or say I don't know, and survive it? Day three hundred forty-six.

A phone buzzes on a table. Three people at dinner glance at it, including the person who swore they weren't going to. Somewhere, someone who designed that buzz is very pleased. Here's a strange way to measure freedom. Not by what you're allowed to do, but by how many hands can tug you. If anyone who can give or withhold what you badly want can move you, then they have a kind of leash on you. Epictetus spent his youth legally owned by another man. He knew what a master was. Today: who holds the leash.
screen: `THE PHONE BUZZES.` → `HOW MANY HANDS CAN TUG YOU?` → `WHO HOLDS THE LEASH.`

segments.voice: First, the foolish wish. Section fourteen opens bluntly. If you want your children and your partner and your friends to live forever, Epictetus says, you're being foolish: you want things that aren't up to you to be up to you. If you want other people never to make mistakes, same problem. He isn't saying don't love them. He's saying don't demand what no one can promise. Second, the definition. Then comes the definition. Each person's master, he says, is whoever has the power to give or take away what that person wants or wants to avoid. That's the leash. Not chains. Wanting. Third, the way out. So whoever wants to be free, he says, should neither want nor avoid anything that depends on others. Otherwise, he says, that person is bound to be a slave. It's a severe word, and he chose it knowing exactly what it meant. Fourth, the leashes we hold out ourselves. Look at what tugs a modern day: a boss's approval, a crush's reply, likes on a post, a parent's praise, a number on a scale. None of those people or things are bad. But each time we let our peace depend on them, we hand someone the end of a leash, often without their asking. Epictetus' point is that a lot of these leashes can be let go of from our end. We can still want the reply. We can just stop needing it. The person holding the other end may never notice. The slack shows up at this end.
screen: `DON'T DEMAND WHAT NO ONE CAN PROMISE.` · `YOUR MASTER: WHOEVER HOLDS WHAT YOU WANT.` · `WANT NOTHING THAT DEPENDS ON OTHERS.` · `THE LEASHES WE HAND OVER.` · then, large: `WHO HOLDS THE LEASH?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and picture your day as a field, with a few leashes trailing from you. Notice where they lead. To a phone. To a person's opinion. To a number. Choose one. Follow it to whoever holds the other end. Ask: what do I want from them that they can give or withhold? Don't cut it yet. Just loosen your own grip on it, a little, and feel the slack. The bell holds the time.
Who holds the leash. Epictetus' measure of freedom: whoever controls what you want or fear is your master, until you let that want go. Today's word.
Your line: who holds the leash. When something tugs you today, a buzz, a look, a number, ask the question, and loosen your end. Day three hundred forty-six.

347.title: Life as a banquet
347.hook: when a dish reaches you, take a modest share; if it passes, don't reach after it (Enchiridion 15)
347.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat good things as dishes passed at a banquet: they take a moderate share when one arrives, and try not to grasp ahead or hold on as it passes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: who holds the leash. That was also your line. When something tugged you, did you loosen your end a little? Day three hundred forty-seven.

A big family dinner. The bowls go around the table, left to right. Mashed potatoes, the good rolls, the one dish everyone fights over. You can see it coming, four people away. There's an uncle who has already half stood up to reach for it. There's a cousin watching it with her fork raised. And there's one person, usually an older aunt, who just talks to whoever's beside her, takes a spoonful when the bowl arrives, and passes it on. Epictetus would have liked that aunt. Section fifteen of the handbook is set at exactly this kind of table. Today: life as a banquet.
screen: `BOWLS GOING AROUND THE TABLE.` → `THE UNCLE HALF STANDING.` → `THE AUNT WHO JUST PASSES IT ON.`

segments.voice: First, the table. Remember, Epictetus says, to behave in life as at a banquet. A dish is carried around and reaches you: put out your hand and take a modest share. Second, the two moments of restraint. It passes you by: don't hold it back. It hasn't come yet: don't send your desire out ahead to meet it. Wait until it's in front of you. That second one is subtle. A lot of our grabbing happens before anything arrives, in our heads, at the promotion we haven't been offered, the house we haven't seen, the relationship we're already planning. Third, what's on the dishes. Do the same, he says, with children, with a spouse, with office, with wealth. They come around. They pass. Take your share well when they reach you. And then, he says, you'll be a worthy guest at the banquet of the gods. He adds a further step, for a few: if you can let some dishes go by even when they're offered, you'll share not just the gods' table but their rule. He names Diogenes the Cynic and Heraclitus as people who lived that way. Fourth, the word. Banquet here is symposion, a drinking together, the same word as Plato's dialogue. Ancient dinners had customs about how the dishes and the cup moved. Epictetus is borrowing manners everyone knew and turning them into a whole philosophy of having. Good things come around. Take a fair share. Pass it on. Don't lean down the table after the next bowl.
screen: `A DISH REACHES YOU: A MODEST SHARE.` · `PASSED: DON'T HOLD IT. NOT YET: WAIT.` · `CHILDREN, OFFICE, WEALTH, ON THE DISHES.` · `SYMPOSION: DRINKING TOGETHER.` · then, large: `WHEN THE DISH COMES.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're reaching ahead for. Something that hasn't come to your end of the table yet: a trip, a result, a bit of good news. Notice your hand, as it were, already stretched toward it. Gently bring the hand back to your lap. Say inside: when the dish comes. Then look at what's in front of you right now, this breath, this chair, this moment, and take a modest share of it. The bell holds the time.
Life as a banquet. Epictetus' table manners for living: take a modest share when the dish reaches you, let it pass, and don't reach ahead. Today's word.
Your line: when the dish comes. Take a modest share of one thing today, food, praise, time, and pass the rest along. Day three hundred forty-seven.

348.title: Beside the weeping
348.hook: sit with a grieving friend and sigh with them, but don't groan inside; some readers find this cool, others wise (Enchiridion 16)
348.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism comfort the grieving with real warmth in word and gesture while trying to stay inwardly steady, so they can keep showing up.

segments.voice: Yesterday: life as a banquet. Your line was when the dish comes. Did you take a modest share of something and pass the rest along? Day three hundred forty-eight.

Lifeguards learn a hard rule early. When someone is drowning, you don't just leap in and grab them. A panicking swimmer can pull the rescuer under, and then there are two people in trouble instead of one. You go in with a float, you stay on top of the water, and from there you can actually help. Grief can work like deep water. A friend calls, sobbing, and it's easy to dive straight in, until we're crying too hard to hear what they need. Section sixteen of the handbook is about exactly this moment. Today: beside the weeping.
screen: `THE LIFEGUARD'S RULE.` → `TWO IN THE WATER.` → `BESIDE THE WEEPING.`

segments.voice: First, the scene. When you see someone weeping in grief, Epictetus says, because a child has gone far away, or because they've lost their property, don't let the impression carry you off, as if they were truly in the grip of an outside evil. Second, the inner sentence. Have ready, he says, the thought: it isn't the event itself that crushes this person, since someone else meets the same event and isn't crushed. It's their judgment about it. That's day three hundred thirty-seven, dogma, turned toward someone else. Third, the outward part. And yet, he says, don't hesitate to sympathize with them in words, and even, if the moment calls for it, to sigh and groan along with them. Only take care not to groan inwardly as well. Sit with them. Speak gently. Just don't drown. Fourth, the two readings. Some people find this passage cool, even a little false: comforting someone while privately thinking their grief is a mistake. Others find it wise and practical, the lifeguard's float: you stay steady enough to stay present, to bring soup on day four, to call again in a month. Epictetus himself doesn't tell you to say the inner sentence out loud. That would be cruel, and nothing in the text suggests it. Neighbors have their own words for the outward part. Paul's letter to the Romans, in the King James words: "weep with them that weep." Epictetus pairs that outward part with a steady one inside.
screen: `SOMEONE WEEPING IN GRIEF.` · `INSIDE: NOT THE EVENT, THE JUDGMENT.` · `OUTSIDE: SIGH WITH THEM.` · `COOL, OR WISE?` · then, large: `WITH THEM, STEADY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you know who is hurting right now. Picture sitting beside them. Let your face soften. Let real sympathy come, the kind you'd show. Then, underneath, find your own feet. Feel the floor, feel your breath going in and out, steady. Two things at once: warmth on the outside, ground on the inside. If you like, decide one small thing you could do for them this week. The bell holds the time.
Beside the weeping. Epictetus on comfort: sigh with a grieving friend, sympathize in words, but keep steady inside, so you can stay. Today's word.
Your line: with them, steady. When someone brings you their trouble today, give them your warmth and keep your feet on the floor. Day three hundred forty-eight.

349.title: An actor in a play
349.hook: you're an actor in a play someone else wrote; your job is to play the part well (Enchiridion 17)
349.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism think of their circumstances as a role they didn't choose, and put their effort into playing it well.

segments.voice: Yesterday: beside the weeping. Your line was with them, steady. When someone brought you their trouble, could you be warm and grounded at once? Day three hundred forty-nine.

The school play is cast, and a kid who wanted the lead is the third tree from the left. One version of that kid sulks through every rehearsal. Another decides to be the best third tree the school has ever seen. Swaying in the wind on cue. Rustling at the sad part. The parents in the audience notice that tree. Nobody chose their role, and the play didn't care. What they did with it was theirs. Epictetus took the theater and made it a picture of a life. Today: an actor in a play.
screen: `THE THIRD TREE FROM THE LEFT.` → `SULK, OR SWAY ON CUE.` → `AN ACTOR IN A PLAY.`

segments.voice: First, the picture. Remember, Epictetus says in section seventeen, that you are an actor in a play, and the play is as the author wants it. If short, then short. If long, then long. Second, the parts. If the author wants you to play a poor man, play even that one well. Or someone lame, or an official, or a private citizen. He lists them flatly, beggar and governor side by side, as if they were just costumes. Third, the line that splits the work. Your business, he says, is to play the given part well. Choosing the part belongs to another. Who is the author? The section doesn't say. Elsewhere Epictetus speaks of God or Zeus; some modern readers hear nature, or circumstance, or simply the hand you were dealt. Either way, the split is the same. Casting isn't yours. Acting is. Fourth, the word. The Greek for actor was hypokrites. English took it over and it slid into hypocrite: someone acting a part that isn't true. Epictetus means the opposite. Play your part truly, with your whole self. Centuries later Shakespeare wrote: "All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players". Epictetus puts the weight elsewhere: merely, maybe, but the playing is everything you get to do. Parent, patient, new hire, caregiver, the one who stayed home this year. If someone hands you the third tree, sway like you mean it.
screen: `THE PLAY IS AS THE AUTHOR WANTS.` · `A POOR MAN, A RULER, PLAY IT WELL.` · `CASTING ISN'T YOURS; ACTING IS.` · `HYPOKRITES: THE ACTOR.` · then, large: `PLAY THE PART WELL.`

segments.voice: Name today's part, plainly, the way a program would list it. Maybe: tired parent. New employee. Patient in a waiting room. Friend who has to say something hard. Don't judge whether it's a good part. Just name it. Then picture one scene ahead of you today, and see yourself playing it well: the tone of voice, the small gesture, the line delivered kindly. Breathe, and step into the role. The bell holds the time.
An actor in a play. Epictetus' picture of a life: the part is given, short or long, rich or poor; your work is to play it well. Today's word.
screen: `AN ACTOR IN A PLAY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: play the part well. Whatever role today hands you, even the third tree, give it your best performance. Day three hundred forty-nine.

350.title: The raven croaks
350.hook: when a raven croaks an omen, remember no sign has power over your will (Enchiridion 18)
350.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners meet a bad omen or ominous news by reminding themselves that it concerns outer things, not their own choices, and asking what good they can draw from what comes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: an actor in a play. Your line was play the part well. Which part did today hand you, and how did you play it? Day three hundred fifty, the end of a week.

A raven calls from a rooftop just as someone sets out on a journey. In Epictetus' world, that harsh croak could be read as a warning, an omen about the trip ahead. The handbook takes that moment seriously enough to give it a whole section. We have our own versions. The text that just says, we need to talk. The dream that leaves a bad taste all morning. The black cat, the broken mirror, the gloomy forecast for the big day. Something small shows up, and it feels like a message about everything. Today: the raven croaks.
screen: `A RAVEN ON THE ROOF.` → `WE NEED TO TALK.` → `THE RAVEN CROAKS.`

segments.voice: First, the moment. When a raven croaks an unlucky omen, Epictetus says in section eighteen, don't let the impression carry you away. Second, the sorting. Instead, divide it at once, and say to yourself: none of this is a sign for me. It may be a sign about my poor body, or my property, or my reputation, or my children or my wife. But not about me, the part that chooses. Notice he doesn't say omens are nonsense. Elsewhere in the handbook he treats consulting a diviner as something people did, with its own proper limits, and we'll meet that in a couple of weeks. His point is narrower: whatever a sign might mean for the things outside you, it can't reach your will. Third, the surprising turn. For me, he says, every sign is a good one, if I want it to be. Whatever comes of it, it's up to me to draw some benefit from it. A bad harvest, a lost case, a scandal: each one is material for patience or courage or honesty. The raven can croak whatever it likes. Fourth, our ravens. The text that says we need to talk often just means a talk. The bad dream was a dream. Even when the sign is right and trouble comes, Epictetus' sorting still holds: it touches the outer pile, not the inner one. And a look back at the week: the price of calm, content to seem foolish, the leash, the banquet, beside the weeping, the actor, and today the raven. Seven ways of keeping the inner pile your own.
screen: `DON'T BE CARRIED AWAY.` · `NO SIGN FOR ME, ONLY MY OUTER THINGS.` · `EVERY SIGN IS GOOD, IF I WISH.` · `OUR RAVENS.` · then, large: `JUST A BIRD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one bad omen from this week. A message, a dream, a feeling about tomorrow, a number that looked wrong. Let it croak once in your mind. Notice the little lurch it brings.
